title: I like the sea
title_target: Μου αρέσει η θάλασσα — Moo ah-reh-see ee thah-lah-sah
goal: Say what you like and dislike — with a sentence pattern that flips everything around: the thing liked becomes the subject, and the person who likes it becomes the target.
bekal: use μου αρέσει and μου αρέσουν correctly
remember that the noun must take an article
use μου αρέσει να for activities
recognize other verbs built the same way

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Likes and dislikes
dialogs.intro: Nikos sounds out Ana's opinion on all things Greek. Notice the verb switching between **αρέσει** and **αρέσουν** — and what decides it isn't who likes, but how many things are liked.

notes: ⚠️ **This is the strangest pattern in the whole module.** *Μου αρέσει ο καφές* is literally "coffee pleases me". The thing liked — coffee — is the **subject**, and the person who likes it stands in front as the **target**. English does the exact opposite: *I* is the subject, *coffee* the object. (Spanish *me gusta* works like Greek.)

**The direct result: the verb follows the THING, not the person.** One thing → **αρέσει**. Several things → **αρέσουν**. *Μου αρέσ**ει** ο καφές* but *Μου αρέσ**ουν** οι ελιές*. ⚠️ This mistake often survives up to B1, because the ear keeps looking for agreement with "I".

**What changes with the person is the little word in front**: **μου** αρέσει (I like), **σου** αρέσει (you like), **του / της** αρέσει (he / she likes), **μας** αρέσει (we like), **σας** αρέσει (you all like), **τους** αρέσει (they like). These are exactly the possessive words from unit 10 — only the position differs: in front, not after.
**The noun must take an article.** *Μου αρέσει **ο** καφές*, not *μου αρέσει καφές*. Greek uses the article for things spoken of in general — where English says just "I like coffee" with no article.

**To name a third person who likes something, use σε + name**: *Στη γιαγιά μου δεν αρέσει ο καφές.* — literally "to my grandmother coffee is not pleasing". It feels heavy at first and natural after ten tries.

**For activities, use μου αρέσει να + verb.** *Μου αρέσει να κολυμπάω.* The verb follows the person as usual: *Σου αρέσει να **διαβάζεις**;* ⚠️ Note that here αρέσει is always singular, however many activities you list.
**Καθόλου** (*kah-THOH-loo*) = "at all", always with δεν. *Δεν μου αρέσει καθόλου.* Its opposite is **πάρα πολύ**. In between come **αρκετά** (quite) and **λίγο** (a little).

**Other verbs built the same way**, all common: **μου λείπει** (I miss), **μου φαίνεται** (it seems to me), **μου πάει** (it suits me, of clothes), **με ενδιαφέρει** (I'm interested), **μου αρκεί** (it's enough for me). Master αρέσει and you master all five at once.

grammars.title: Μου αρέσει — the full table
body: Read the "literally" column slowly, once. After that, forget it and learn each chunk as a single unit.
after: **Negating:** δεν goes first, before the little word. *Δεν μου αρέσει.* — I don't like it. For emphasis: *Δεν μου αρέσει **καθόλου**.*
**Asking back:** *Σου αρέσει;* — do you like it? Short answers: **Μου αρέσει!** or **Δεν μου αρέσει.** ⚠️ Just *Ναι* isn't enough; Greeks expect the verb to be repeated.

grammars.title: Degrees of liking and disliking
body: From strongest liking to strongest rejection. Note that the two extremes use the ordinary pattern, not the flipped one.

after: ⚠️ **Μου αρέσει often shortens to μ' αρέσει** in fast speech, and likewise *σ' αρέσει*. You'll hear these far more often than the long forms.
**Λατρεύω** literally "I worship", is used for food, places, and songs without sounding over the top. It's a cousin of the *-latry* in English *idolatry*.

sections.title: Things people commonly like and dislike

blocks.title: Four more verbs that flip their subject
items: **Μου λείπει / μου λείπουν** — I miss. *Μου λείπει η οικογένειά μου.* — I miss my family. ⚠️ Literally "my family is lacking to me" — a more exact picture than "miss" will ever give.
**Μου φαίνεται** — it seems to me. *Μου φαίνεται καλή ιδέα.* — Sounds like a good idea to me. *Μου φαίνεται πως …* — It looks like …
**Μου πάει** — it suits me (clothes, colors, a haircut). *Σου πάει αυτό το χρώμα!* — That color suits you!
**Με ενδιαφέρει** — I'm interested. *Με ενδιαφέρει η ιστορία.* — I'm interested in history. Note that this one uses **με**, not **μου** — a small group that takes the ordinary object form.
